Planning the trip

A trip to a Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting competition starts with its programme. It gives the dates, the disciplines, the deadline for entry and the entry fee. You enter through the organiser. Popular events can fill up long before the deadline, so do not leave it late.

Look for a place to stay near the ground. Shooting often starts early, and a long drive each day takes energy. Organisers often suggest partner hotels. Book early, and ask the hotel whether it accepts guests with sporting guns and where a gun can be kept safely.

Plan the transfers: from the airport to the hotel, and from the hotel to the ground each day. A hire car gives freedom, but carrying a gun by car has its own rules in each country. A taxi may refuse a passenger with a gun, and some competitions run a shuttle for shooters.

Documents for the gun and the cartridges take the longest to prepare. Start several weeks ahead, and even earlier for a trip outside the EU: Travelling with a gun inside the EU, Outside the EU: national permits and Flying with a gun. If taking your own gun is too complicated, ask the ground whether it hires out guns.

Try to arrive a day or two early. Shooting times are given in local time. After a flight across several time zones, your body may need more days: see Jet lag and the first days at a new ground.

An early arrival also leaves time to practise. Where you may practise depends on the discipline.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Before the competition, nobody may practise on the competition layouts — the stands set up for the event. You can practise on other parts of the ground (Chapter 15 · No practice on competition layouts).

Compak® Sporting

You may practise on the target flights (trajectories) of the competition, but under a different setting table: the plan of which traps are shot from each station. So you do not practise the exact combination you will shoot (Chapter 6 · Practice on competition trajectories). At continental and world championships, official practice opens on the Saturday before the championship (Chapter 6 · Championships: official practice from the Saturday before).

On each shooting day, be at the ground early, because being late means lost targets. In Sporting™, the targets you were not there for are scored as zeros (Chapter 16 · Late or absent shooter). In Compak® Sporting it is stricter: a late shooter gets 25 zeros, a whole round. When you shoot in a squad (a group that goes through the round together), you are late once the first shooter of your squad has called the first target (Chapter 9 · Late in squad shooting: 25 zeros).

Tip: A short checklist: documents, insurance, ear and eye protection, clothes for the weather, the programme in local time and the organiser's contacts. Spare time is good insurance too.

Key points

  • Enter early: popular events fill up.
  • Stay near the ground and ask the hotel where to keep the gun.
  • Start on gun documents weeks ahead, and earlier for trips outside the EU.
  • Arrive a day or two early; shooting times are in local time.
  • Practice before the event: in Sporting™, away from the competition layouts; in Compak® Sporting, on the competition targets but under a different setting table (plan of traps per station).
  • Pack documents, insurance, ear and eye protection and clothes for the weather.

Did you know?

Shooting times can move during an event when there are delays. In Compak® Sporting, the rules make following these changes the shooter's own job (Chapter 8 · Shooting schedule: the shooter's responsibility).

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which statement about practice before a competition is true?

    1. In Sporting™ you may practise on the competition layouts
    2. In Compak® Sporting you may not practise at all before the competition
    3. In Sporting™ you may practise only on other parts of the ground
    Answer

    In Sporting™ you may practise only on other parts of the ground

    In Sporting™ the competition layouts are closed to practice, so you practise on other parts of the ground. In Compak® Sporting you may practise on the competition target flights under a different setting table; at championships, official practice opens on the Saturday before the championship.

    Chapter 15 · No practice on competition layouts

  2. Why plan to arrive a day or two before the competition?

    1. To settle in, adjust to local time and practise
    2. To pay a smaller entry fee for arriving early
    3. To choose your own squad and starting time
    Answer

    To settle in, adjust to local time and practise

    The body needs time after a long trip, and an early arrival lets you prepare calmly.

  3. In which time are the shooting times given?

    1. In the time of your home country
    2. In the local time at the venue
    3. In UTC, the same in all countries
    Answer

    In the local time at the venue

    The schedule is in local time, so check your phone's clock after the flight.
